I had a whole alternative sketched in my head while she was talking, a lighter-weight check that would still catch the critical stuff.

Didn't say it though. The senior architects set up the current flow and they were in the call. Felt like bringing up a redesign right there would come across as me trying to show off, especially with the tech lead thing floating around. So I just nodded and said I could look into Devika's point offline. She seemed a bit deflated that nobody backed her up more directly. I get it.

Weird day. Started normal — coffee, standup, tickets. Then around lunch Pieter from platform team pinged me about a side project he's been hacking on, this internal tool for tracking deployment health across services. He wanted to know if I'd help build the backend. Not sanctioned work, just something he thinks would be useful and wants to pitch to leadership once it's built.

First thought was yes obviously, this is the kind of thing I actually want to spend time on, building something new without twelve layers of sign-off. Second thought was that Martijn would not love me spending cycles on an unsanctioned project right when he's evaluating me for lead. Third thought was that Pieter didn't ask anyone else, he asked me, and that felt good in a way I don't fully understand. Like someone saw the part of me that wants to just build.

I told Pieter I'd think about it over the weekend. Which is code for "I want to do it but I need to figure out if I'm allowed to want to do it." That sounds ridiculous written down. I'm a grown man deciding whether to write some code on the side. But it feels more loaded than that right now.

Martijn officially put me on the lead shortlist. Two candidates, me and someone from the other squad. I thanked him and said I'd put my best foot forward. Which I will. Whatever doubts I have aren't anyone else's problem to carry.

Told Pieter I'd help with the tool. We set up a repo and I spent an hour last night after Noor went to sleep scaffolding the API layer. Felt more engaged in that hour than I have all sprint on the actual work.

Today was back to normal though — reviewing PRs, answering Slack threads, sitting through a planning session where half the decisions had already been made before we walked in. The usual. I'm not complaining, it's fine. I just noticed the contrast, that's all.

Noor and I went to dinner with her parents in Rotterdam on Saturday. Her dad asked about the promotion and I gave the standard answer — it's in progress, I'm grateful for the opportunity, etc. He seemed pleased. On the train back Noor said she was proud of me and I felt genuinely good about it. Like I'm on a track that makes sense to the people I care about.

Then on Sunday I stayed up way too late working on Pieter's tool and got completely absorbed refactoring the data ingestion layer. Noor asked what I was doing and I said "just work stuff" which wasn't really a lie but wasn't the whole truth either. I don't know why I didn't just explain it. Maybe because explaining it would mean admitting how much more alive that project makes me feel, and then someone might ask what that says about everything else.
Presented the deployment health tool to Pieter's skip-level manager today. She liked it. Asked if we'd want to bring it under the platform roadmap officially. Said yes without hesitating.

Team drinks after work. Everyone was congratulating me about the shortlist like it's already decided. I kept saying it wasn't confirmed yet but nobody listens. Devika made a joke about me being her future boss and I laughed but it sat wrong with me for the rest of the evening.

I don't think I'm being fake about it. I genuinely want to do well, and the role comes with better pay, more visibility, things that matter. But there's this gap between how I talk about it to other people and what actually runs through my head at 11pm when I'm staring at Pieter's repo. Not sure what to do with that. For now I'm doing both, which is sustainable enough.

Still thinking about the mansaf. The thing that keeps coming back to me is that she learned all of it here, in this kitchen, from watching me. Which means even if she's somewhere else, she carries it. I don't know why that's so hard for me to trust.

My father never let any of us leave Amman until we were married. I accepted that. But I also remember the years I spent wondering what it would have been like to study abroad when I had the chance. I told myself it didn't matter because I had responsibilities. Maybe it didn't matter. Or maybe I just never forgave myself for not pushing harder, and now I'm doing the same thing to her.

My brother Walid called and said I should let Noor go, that I'm being selfish. Easy for him to say from Dubai with his kids in boarding school. Nobody in this family understands that keeping people close isn't the same as holding them back.

Spent the morning making maamoul with Hana and Tariq. They came over early, flour everywhere, the kitchen smelled like the house used to when Samira was alive. Hana shaped hers exactly the way her mother did, pressing the mold with both palms. I watched her and something settled inside me, like proof that what I've kept going all these years still matters to them too.

Tariq asked if we could do this every Friday, not just during holidays. I said of course. Small thing, but it sat well with me the rest of the afternoon.
Noor brought up the London program again at dinner. I could feel my chest tighten but I just said we'd talk later and cleared the plates. Haven't been able to sleep since.

Noor cooked mansaf tonight. The whole thing, from scratch, without asking for help. She set the platter on the table the way I always do, rice shaped just right. Felt like she was showing me something without saying it.

Came back to this tonight because Walid's call kept eating at me. After I hung up I sat in the garden for a long time. The jasmine Samira planted is still growing along the back wall, fifteen years now. I thought about how she would have handled this. She was always braver about letting the children try things. I think she would have been scared too but she wouldn't have let the fear win.

I don't know if that changes what I'll say to Noor. But I realized the anger I felt toward Walid was really just the sound of my own doubt getting louder.

Eid preparations started today and the house was full. Hana brought her husband and the baby, Tariq came with sweets from that bakery on Rainbow Street, even Walid video-called from Dubai to wish us well. Noor was in the kitchen all morning helping me roll grape leaves. For a few hours it felt exactly right, all the noise, the food, children running through every room. This is what I stayed home for.

But then after everyone left and it was just Noor and me cleaning up, she said quietly that she'd been offered a partial scholarship. She wasn't asking permission, not exactly, more like she was letting me know it was real now. I didn't say anything. I just kept drying the dishes and stacking them slowly.

I know I need to talk to her. I know what I'm leaning toward. But saying it out loud makes it final in a way I'm not ready for. The house will be so quiet without her.

I told her it was methodologically sound and left it at that. I don't owe anyone an explanation for why this subject matters to me. She's Swedish. She studies migration patterns. My brother Faisal made a comment at Friday lunch about how I'm "still playing student" while his sons are already building careers. His eldest is twenty-six and works at a bank. I smiled and passed the hummus. But it wouldn't have been the right moment. My mother was sitting right there, and she gets anxious when Faisal and I disagree. So I stayed quiet, helped clear the plates, and drove home listening to Fairuz with the windows down. The breeze off the hills felt good. I don't need Faisal's approval. I know what I'm doing and why.

Interesting thing happened during morning assembly. One of my Class 3 students, Ravi, came up to me after and said he told his mother about the water pollution lesson I did last week. She apparently asked him to explain it again because their neighborhood has been complaining about the nala running brown. He was so proud of himself, like he'd done something important.

And maybe he did? A nine-year-old going home and talking to his family about why their water is dirty—that feels like something actually working. Not in a big dramatic way, just a small thread pulling in the right direction. I changed nothing about anyone's pipes but now one family is paying attention. That's enough for today.

Went to the literacy camp in Sultanpur today and I keep thinking about this one girl, maybe seven or eight, who was holding the pencil like she'd never held one before. And honestly she probably hadn't. She was gripping it so tight her knuckles were white and she kept looking at me like she was asking permission to write her own name.

I sat with her for almost an hour. The other volunteers were doing group activities but I just couldn't move on from this kid. Her name is Fatima. She got the first two letters right and then she looked at me and smiled and it was like, okay, this is why I wake up early on Saturdays and take that awful bus that takes ninety minutes one way.

I know this sounds naive or whatever. Didi would say I'm romanticizing things. But I was there today and she wasn't. There's something about being in the room with someone who just learned they can write their own name that makes all the other noise—the salary complaints, Baba asking when I'll "move up," the crumbling school building—feel small. Not irrelevant, just not the point.

Spent the afternoon at the refugee clinic. There was a Syrian woman, maybe my age, who came in with chronic back pain that's been ignored for months because she keeps getting shuffled between GP practices and nobody follows through. When she left she squeezed my hand and said something in Arabic I didn't understand but I could tell what it meant.

Those moments remind me why I do what I do. It's not heroic, it's just basic decency — making sure someone gets the care they should have had weeks ago. The system fails these people constantly and most of the time there's nobody there to catch them. I can't fix everything but I can make sure the ones who come through my door don't fall through the cracks.

Walked home along the Maas afterwards and the late afternoon light on the water was beautiful. Felt like myself for the first time all week. Made a simple stamppot for dinner and sat in the garden with a glass of wine and the radio on. Days like this keep me going.

Saturday. Slept in which I almost never do. Made coffee and read the Volkskrant at the kitchen table like I used to when the kids were small, except now the house is quiet and nobody's fighting over the last beschuit.

The paper had a big piece about plastic pollution in the North Sea and it got me going again. They found microplastics in fish at the market in Scheveningen. I remember swimming there as a girl and the water was already dirty then, but at least we weren't eating the pollution. Now it's in everything. I want to feel like individual choices matter — I bring my own bags, I cycle, I sort my recycling obsessively — but these articles make it feel so small against the scale of it. Shell is right there across the river and they're still doing what they've always done.

Went grocery shopping after, argued with myself about buying the organic tomatoes that cost twice as much. Bought them anyway. Had a quiet afternoon fixing the hem on my uniform trousers and listening to a podcast about healthcare in sub-Saharan Africa. Normal day really. Nothing remarkable.

Had a terrible shift today and I can't stop going over it. We had a team meeting about the new triage protocols and someone — one of the younger consultants — made a comment about how we should be "more selective" about which patients get palliative referrals because the ward is overstretched. He was basically implying we should deprioritise patients who don't have family pushing for it, which in practice means the homeless patients, the migrants, the people nobody's advocating for. I sat there and I knew exactly what he meant and I said nothing. A few people nodded. Anke looked uncomfortable but she didn't speak up either.

I've been doing this work for thirty years and I just let it slide. I told myself it was because the meeting was already running long and tempers were short, but honestly I think I was just tired. Tired and afraid of being that older nurse who's always making everything political. But those are real people he was talking about, people I've held hands with while they died. Nobody should have to earn the right to a dignified death by having relatives who make enough noise.

I'm angry at myself. I keep rehearsing what I should have said and it's making my stomach hurt. Willem would tell me to let it go and pick my battles, but this feels like exactly the kind of battle I should have picked.

Back from the conference for a week now and people at work keep asking how it was. I say it was great, very inspiring, lots of good ideas. Which is true. But when they ask what I am going to do differently, I do not have a good answer. Learn Go? Propose a rewrite? Those feel like someone else's moves.

My manager suggested I do a lunch-and-learn to share what I learned. I said I would think about it. I probably will not do it. Public speaking was never my thing, and honestly, the sessions that meant most to me were the ones I cannot really present in a corporate setting. Nobody wants a slide deck about existential uncertainty in late-career engineers.

December sprint started with three people out sick and a scope increase nobody agreed to. I have been working ten-hour days trying to keep us on track for the holiday release. Jennifer is frustrated because her Go rewrite keeps getting deprioritized. I am frustrated because I am the one who has to explain why to her without making leadership look bad.

Had dinner with Elena's cousin Miguel who is visiting from Monterrey. He runs a small construction company there. He asked me about my job and I tried to explain sprint planning and stakeholder management and he just laughed and said it sounds like I spend a lot of energy managing people's feelings about work instead of actually working. He did not mean it unkindly but it stuck with me. Maybe he is right. Maybe that is what corporate software engineering becomes after a while.
The morning after a bad night is always strange. Everything looks normal. Coffee tastes the same. I just feel like I am watching myself go through the motions from somewhere slightly outside.

The new architect they brought in, Jennifer, she wants to rewrite the payment gateway from scratch. Using Go instead of Java. Everyone in the room looked at me like I was supposed to object, since I built the original thing in 2019. But honestly? Part of me wanted to say yes, let us do it, let me learn something new instead of patching the same codebase forever.

I did not say that though. I said we should consider the timeline and the risk to the December release. Which is true. The business needs stability. But I walked out of that meeting feeling like I had swallowed something heavy.

Long day. Production incident at 3 AM, the payment gateway again. Not the part Jennifer wanted to rewrite, ironically, but the legacy integration with the bank's SFTP server. I was on call so I got the page. Took four hours to trace it to a certificate expiration that nobody had on their calendar.

By 7 AM I had fixed it and documented everything. By 8 AM I was in the standup explaining what happened. By 9 AM I was getting messages from the VP asking how we let this happen. Not thank you for catching it. Not good job on the quick fix. Just how did we let this happen.

I did not let anything happen. I inherited this system. I have been asking for budget to modernize the certificate management for two years. But I did not say that either. I just said we would add better monitoring and put the renewal dates in a shared calendar. Safe answer. Team player answer.

Elena asked me at dinner why I looked so tired. I said work was busy. I did not tell her about the VP message because then she would get angry on my behalf and I would have to either agree with her anger or defend the company that made me feel small today. Both options felt exhausting.

I need to sleep but my mind keeps rehearsing the incident like I missed something. I did not miss anything. The certificate was not in any documentation I had access to. But I keep checking anyway.

Flew to San Francisco yesterday for the unconference. Staying at a hotel near the Embarcadero with a view of the bay. Weather is cold and gray but I brought my good jacket.

The conference format is interesting. You show up in the morning, people pitch sessions on index cards, everyone votes with stickers, and then the schedule emerges. No predetermined speakers, no approved slides. Someone proposed a session on rebuilding legacy systems with LLMs. Someone else wanted to discuss leaving tech after 50. I almost proposed something about maintaining software versus maintaining yourself, but I did not have the index card ready in time.

I attended four sessions. The legacy systems one was good, practical advice I could use. The leaving tech one was harder to sit through. A woman around my age talked about how she realized she had optimized her whole life for a company that laid her off in an afternoon. She cried a little. Everyone was respectful.

Tonight I walked along the waterfront instead of joining the dinner group. Watched the ferries come and go. Called my mother. She asked if I was eating well and I said yes, even though I had skipped lunch. Some lies are kindness.

Tomorrow is the last day. I feel different here. Not better or worse. Just different.
Another sprint planning meeting where they want me to estimate the same maintenance tickets I have been doing for three years. I know exactly how long everything takes now. That is maybe the problem.

Elena surprised me with tickets to a tech conference in San Francisco next month. Not the corporate kind with vendor booths and networking bingo, but one of those unconference events where people just propose sessions in the morning and see what happens. She said she noticed I have been looking at conference websites lately but never registering for anything.

I should be excited. Five years ago I would have booked the flight before she finished her sentence. Now I am already thinking about the sprint commitments, about whether Marcus can handle the on-call rotation alone, about what my manager will say when I request the days off. The conference is on a weekend. I would only need to take Friday off. Still, I hesitated.

What bothers me most is not the hesitation itself. It is that I used to make decisions faster. Move to Austin? Two weeks to decide. Take the startup job over the stable bank position? One evening with Elena and a bottle of wine. Now I research, I weigh, I consider all stakeholders. My mother would say I finally grew up. But it feels more like something got dimmer.

I will go to the conference. I already told Elena yes. I just wish the yes had come easier.

She didn't separate them at first, just collecting, and then she looked at her bucket and said the plastic ones aren't pretty. I asked what we should do with them and she said throw them away properly. We spent another thirty minutes walking to find recycling and trash bins.

It's a small thing. A kid picking up beach trash. But watching her make that distinction on her own, without being told, reminded me of why Mei Ling and I try to live the way we do. Not because we're going to fix the ocean or the climate or anything so grand, but because the habits matter. The noticing matters.

Came home and cooked dinner together, the three of us. Xiao Yu was in charge of washing vegetables. She takes the job very seriously, inspecting each leaf. Mei Ling and I exchanged a look over her head, the kind of look that says we might be doing okay at this. It's been an exhausting few weeks but tonight I feel settled in a way I haven't for a while.

He showed me the bruises on his back, purple-yellow, still swelling around his ribs. I helped him draft a letter to MOM. My Mandarin-accented English and his Tamil-accented English, both of us stumbling through legalese neither of us was built for.

Family group chat exploded today. My uncle Hernando posted a news article about the Guaviare deforestation — same issue the march is about — and wrote "sad but what can you do, these people need to eat." I started typing a response three times. Deleted all of them.

It's not that I disagree entirely — the economics of it are real and I've seen the poverty firsthand. But the framing drives me insane. "What can you do" as if there are no choices, no policies, no one responsible. I wanted to write about the logging companies, the lack of enforcement, the families who actually live there being displaced. But Hernando is my mother's brother and I can already picture the awkward silence at Easter dinner if I go off in the group chat.

So I sent a sad emoji and closed the app. Mature. Professional. Utterly hollow. Patricia would have posted a five-paragraph essay with citations. I admire that and also cannot imagine being that person in my own family. The mural for the march — that I can do. Words in the chat where my grandmother can see them — that's different somehow, and I hate that it's different.

Good day at the workshop. One of the teenagers, David, showed up with a collage about his neighborhood flooding last year — garbage and river water mixed together. He made it beautiful without sanitizing it. I wish I had his nerve sometimes.
Long day prepping supplies for Friday. Shoulders ache. Didn't think about the committee or my mother or the march. Just mixed pigments and cleaned brushes. Sometimes that's enough.

Can't sleep. Kept redoing the sketch for the Suba district mural because the committee wants something "uplifting" and every version I draw keeps drifting toward the river contamination. My hand knows what it wants to make but the brief says otherwise.

My mother called. Someone told her about the march mural. She didn't yell — she never yells — she just got very quiet and asked "is this going to be a problem for you?" That question does more damage than yelling ever could.

Meeting with Patricia from the environmental collective went better than expected. She's organizing a march next month about the deforestation in Guaviare and wants muralists to paint temporary pieces along the route. No committee, no brief, no polite rewrites — just paint what you see and feel. I said yes before I finished my coffee.

Spent the afternoon looking at satellite images of the cleared areas. It's staggering how fast the green disappears between one photo and the next. I started sketching a piece that layers the satellite view underneath a portrait of a family I met two years ago when I traveled there for a residency. They had this small farm at the edge of the forest. I keep wondering if that farm still exists.

The march is February 28. Patricia asked if I'd also speak at the rally beforehand. I told her I'd think about it. Speaking is different from painting — you can't hide behind brushstrokes. My mother would probably tell me to just do the mural and not draw attention to myself. She still worries about artists getting into trouble. But Patricia's right that the work means more when the person behind it shows up.

The Suba mural committee approved a revised design. I compromised — kept the river but softened the contamination imagery into something more abstract. Flowing blues and greens instead of the murky brown I originally wanted. They loved it. Said it was "inspiring." I nodded and thanked everyone and then sat in my car for ten minutes staring at the steering wheel.

I keep telling myself this is how it works. Public art is negotiation. You serve the community's vision, not just your own. And maybe the abstracted version will still land — maybe someone will look at those blues and sense that something is wrong underneath. That's the hope, anyway. But part of me keeps hearing David's collage in my head, all that directness, no translation required.

Called my cousin Marcela tonight. She's a lawyer in Medellin, very proper, always knows the right thing to say at family dinners. I told her about the march and she got quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Lu, you know how tia Rosa talks. Just be careful what you attach your name to." And I know she means it with love. I know the family worries. But careful has a cost too, and I'm starting to wonder how much it's adding up.
Finished the base layer of the march mural today. It's honest work. Stood back and felt something I haven't felt in a while — that the paint is saying exactly what I mean.

I can't even have a genuine reaction anymore because every interaction is a positioning exercise.

Van der Meer has ambition but I don't trust his judgment yet. Sophie is twenty years from being ready. I tell myself I'm protecting the company from incompetence but maybe I'm protecting myself from being replaced. If someone else can do what I do, then what am I? Just the guy whose name is on the building. I've spent thirty years making sure I was irreplaceable and now that's the problem.

Had dinner with my daughter Annelies tonight. She asked when I'm going to retire. I told her the same thing I always tell her — when I'm ready. She laughed and said I've been saying that for ten years. She's not wrong.

The truth is, I don't know what I would do. The company isn't just a business, it's the structure of my days. It's where I matter. When I walk into that building, people listen. They need my decisions. At home, Marijke has her garden club and her grandchildren schedule and I'm just another person underfoot. She loves me, I know that, but she doesn't need me the way the company does.

Annelies suggested I mentor young entrepreneurs. The idea of sitting in coffee shops giving advice to twenty-five-year-olds who think they invented disruption makes me want to throw something. I don't want to be an elder statesman. I want to be in the fight.

Strange moment today. Young account manager named Sophie presented a new client pitch to me. She was nervous — I could see her hands trembling on her laptop. I remembered being that nervous once, thirty-five years ago, presenting to the board of a shipping company we desperately needed as a client.

I let her finish without interrupting, which is not my usual approach. When she was done I told her the pitch was solid but she needed to slow down and own the silences. She looked at me like I'd handed her a map. That felt good. Different from closing a deal, but good.

Maybe Annelies isn't entirely wrong about the mentoring thing. Just not with strangers in coffee shops.

Can't sleep. Keep thinking about Pieter and Thomas leaving. We worked together for fifteen years. Fifteen years, and they walked into the enemy camp without so much as a conversation first. What does that say about what I built? What does that say about loyalty? Or was it all just leverage, waiting for a better offer?

Quarterly review. Numbers are solid — 8% growth despite the disruption. Told the team they exceeded expectations. Van der Meer apologized for the consultant suggestion. I accepted graciously. Maarten gave me a nod from across the room. Small victories. The company is steady. That's what matters.

Family dinner at Annelies's house. My grandson Lucas asked me what I do all day. I started explaining logistics operations and he interrupted to say his friend's grandfather is retired and takes him fishing every Saturday. Annelies jumped in before I could respond, changed the subject to dessert.

Later Marijke told me I looked hurt. I wasn't hurt. I was annoyed. The comparison is absurd — some retired accountant who goes fishing isn't building something. He's killing time. But I kept thinking about it on the drive home. Lucas is eight. He doesn't know the difference between building and coasting. All he knows is his friend's grandfather has time for him and his doesn't.

The thing is, I could make time. I choose not to because Saturday mornings are when I review the weekly reports uninterrupted. But when I try to explain that maintaining what I've built requires constant attention, even to myself, it starts to sound like an excuse. I'm not sure when protecting the company became a reason to miss everything else.

Back in the hotel room. Skipped the dinner. Couldn't stomach another three hours of strategic smiling. Ordered room service and watched the ceiling. Thirty years and I still have to play these games. When does it end? When do I get to just be somewhere without worrying about who's watching?
